stem: A client with a new colostomy reports burning under the skin barrier. The nurse removes the pouch and finds stool has leaked beneath the barrier and the peristomal skin is red and moist. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Gently cleanse and assess the peristomal skin, refit the barrier opening closely around the stoma, and apply a new pouching system rather than patching the leak with tape.
options.B: Gently cleanse and dry the skin, then reapply the leaking pouch and reinforce the barrier edge with tape so the system can remain in place until the next scheduled change.
options.C: Gently cleanse the skin and cut the new barrier opening noticeably larger than the stoma so the irritated peristomal skin is not compressed by the pouching system.
options.D: Gently cleanse the exposed skin and wait until the next routine pouch change to reassess the fit because mild burning and moisture can be observed if stool output remains contained.

rationale: WOCN identifies stool undermining the skin barrier as a cause of peristomal moisture-associated irritant skin damage. Its clinician guide directs prompt barrier or pouch change when burning or leakage occurs, assessment of the adhesive side and peristomal skin, and sizing of the barrier opening to fit closely around the stoma base. WOCN also specifically states to change a leaking pouch rather than reinforce it with additional tape. Routine peristomal cleansing may be performed gently with clean water. Therefore A is correct. B leaves the failed leaking system in place and patches it with tape. C deliberately exposes more skin to effluent by making the opening too large. D delays reassessment and replacement despite burning, moisture, and documented stool leakage.
educational_objective: When stool leaks beneath a colostomy barrier and causes burning or moist peristomal skin, promptly change the pouching system, assess the skin and barrier fit, and size the barrier opening closely around the stoma rather than patching or delaying care.
source_organization: Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society (WOCN)
source_document_title: Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide for Clinicians; Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide for Consumers
source_locator: Clinician Guide > Peristomal Moisture Associated Skin Damage (PMASD): change the skin barrier promptly for itching/burning or leakage; ensure the skin-barrier opening is sized to fit closely around the stoma base. PMASD-Maceration: effluent undermining the barrier is trapped against peristomal skin and causes damage; assess the adhesive side and fit; change the pouching system whenever there is burning or leakage and do not reinforce with tape. PMASD-Irritant Dermatitis: assess pouching-system fit; change the barrier for burning, itching, or leakage; inspect for stool undermining. Patient Education: cleanse with warm tap water; change pouch for burning, itching, and leakage. Referral/Interim Interventions: change pouch when leaking and do not reinforce with additional tape.
source_claim_supported: Stool leakage beneath an ostomy barrier can cause peristomal moisture-associated irritant skin damage; burning or leakage warrants prompt pouch-system change and skin/barrier assessment, with a closely fitted barrier opening and no tape reinforcement of a leaking pouch.

supporting_sources.organization: Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society (WOCN)
supporting_sources.document_title: Peristomal Skin Assessment Guide for Consumers
supporting_sources.locator: Healthy Peristomal Skin / Tips for Better Skin Care: check barrier/pouching-system fit, change the pouching system for burning or leakage, and cleanse the peristomal skin with warm tap water.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Routine ostomy self-care includes prompt response to burning/leakage and gentle peristomal cleansing.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p. 17: provide ostomy care and education (e.g., tracheal, enteral). Related Basic Care and Comfort activity statements on printed pp. 14 and 35 include performing skin assessment and implementing measures to maintain skin/tissue integrity and assessing/managing alterations in bowel and bladder elimination.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — colostomy pouching-system management and peristomal skin protection
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to remove the uniquely-long keyed answer and make the distractors realistic ostomy-care errors involving tape reinforcement, an oversized barrier opening, and delayed response to leakage. The item was remapped to Physiological Adaptation because the 2026 NCSBN Test Plan directly lists ostomy care and education.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Colostomy care — peristomal irritant skin injury from stool leakage
audit_findings.stem: PASS — burning, documented stool undermining, and red moist peristomal skin create a coherent pouch-fit and skin-protection problem.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly follows WOCN guidance to cleanse/assess, correct the fit, and replace a leaking system rather than patching it; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — cleansing is appropriate, but reapplying a failed leaking pouch and reinforcing it with tape conflicts with WOCN guidance.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — cleansing and changing the system are appropriate concepts, but a larger opening exposes additional peristomal skin to effluent instead of fitting closely around the stoma base.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — cleansing is appropriate, but burning and leakage are explicit indications for prompt pouch-system assessment/change rather than waiting for a routine interval.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that corrects both the active skin exposure and the underlying pouch-fit problem without adding a contradictory step.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B patches a leaking system, C intentionally creates poor fit, and D delays indicated reassessment/change.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options are tightly matched in length and clinical specificity and the keyed answer is not uniquely long.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation explicitly includes ostomy care and education, with related skin-integrity and elimination activities in Basic Care and Comfort.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether tape reinforcement or a wider opening might be acceptable temporary measures; WOCN directly states to change a leaking pouch rather than reinforce it and to size the opening closely around the stoma base, leaving A uniquely best.
